Ethnology is the scientific, comparative study of human cultures — their characteristics, origins, development, similarities, and differences. An ethnologist looks at multiple cultures from around the world and tries to understand why they are the way they are, how they relate to each other, and what patterns emerge when you put them side by side.

Think of it this way: if you were a scientist who studied animals, you wouldn't just describe one animal in detail. You'd compare many animals to understand evolution, behavior, and biology more deeply. Ethnology does the same thing, but with human cultures instead of animals.

Ethnology is not just describing a culture. It goes further — it analyzes and compares cultures. An ethnologist might ask:

  • Why do certain societies develop similar religious rituals even when they've never been in contact with each other?
  • How have trade routes, migration, or war caused cultures to influence one another across centuries?
  • What can the similarities between a family structure in Africa and one in South America tell us about how human societies are organized?
  • How do different cultures solve the same universal human problems — like raising children, organizing government, or dealing with death?

These are not questions you can answer by studying just one culture. You need to examine many and then compare them thoughtfully. That is exactly what ethnology does.
How ethnology is different from ethnography

Since these two words look and sound similar, it's important to know the difference — and once you do, ethnology becomes much clearer.

Ethnography is the detailed, up-close, descriptive study of a single culture or community. An ethnographer lives among a group of people, observes their daily life, records their customs, documents their language, and writes it all down in rich detail. The goal is to understand one culture from the inside.

Ethnology takes the work done by ethnographers — about many different cultures — and uses it as raw material for comparison and analysis. Ethnology zooms out and asks: "Now that we have detailed descriptions of hundreds of different cultures, what can we learn when we look at them all together?"

So ethnography = deep description of one culture.
Ethnology = comparison and analysis of many cultures.

One feeds the other. Ethnology depends on ethnographic research, but it goes beyond simple description toward theory-building and explanation.

Ethnologists examine nearly every aspect of human cultural life, including:

  • Social structures — how families, clans, and communities are organized; rules about marriage; how power is distributed
  • Religion and belief systems — myths, rituals, sacred objects, ideas about the afterlife
  • Language and communication — not just the words, but how language reflects a culture's worldview
  • Technology and material culture — the tools, objects, and technologies a culture develops
  • Economic systems — how cultures produce, share, and trade goods
  • History and migration — how peoples moved across the globe and how their cultures changed as a result

The goal is not just to collect these facts, but to make sense of them — to find patterns, build theories, and explain why human cultures develop in the ways they do.
Ethnology's place in the world of knowledge

Ethnology is a branch of anthropology (the broad study of humanity). In many European countries and academic traditions, "ethnology" and "cultural anthropology" are used almost interchangeably, since both deal with the comparative study of cultures. In the United States, the distinction is sometimes drawn more sharply, with ethnology treated as a subfield focused specifically on comparison and historical relationships between cultures.

Ethnology has been practiced in a formal, academic sense since the 19th century, but humans have been comparing and reflecting on cultural differences since ancient times. What modern ethnology adds is scientific rigor, systematic methods, and an ethical commitment to studying cultures with respect and without bias.

Ethnology teaches us something fundamental: that human beings, despite living in vastly different environments and building vastly different societies, share deep commonalities. It also shows us that there is no single "correct" way to organize a society, raise children, or understand the world. By studying cultures comparatively, ethnology expands our understanding of what it means to be human.

It has also had very practical applications — influencing policies on indigenous rights, informing humanitarian work, shaping how governments interact with minority cultures, and challenging the false assumption that any one culture is inherently superior to another.
How the word is used in sentences

• "Her research in ethnology focused on the similarities between funeral rites in ancient Egypt and pre-Columbian Mexico."
  • "The museum's department of ethnology maintains one of the world's largest collections of cultural artifacts."
  • "Ethnology teaches us that customs which seem strange to outsiders almost always make deep sense within their own cultural context."
  • "He studied ethnology because he wanted to understand not just individual cultures, but the larger story of humanity as a whole."

Ethnology is the scientific, comparative study of human cultures — examining their similarities, differences, origins, and relationships in order to understand the full range of human experience and what it means to live together as a society.
